name: Simón Bolívar
info: Simón Bolívar (1783–1830) was a Venezuelan military officer and statesman, known as El Libertador, who led what are now Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru and Venezuela to independence from the Spanish Empire.

facts.born: 24 July 1783 in Caracas, capital of the Captaincy General of Venezuela; fourth and youngest child of Juan Vicente Bolívar y Ponte and María de la Concepción Palacios y Blanco, one of the wealthiest criollo families in the Spanish Americas
facts.died: 17 December 1830, aged 47, of tuberculosis, at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino near Santa Marta
facts.role: Dictator of the Second Republic of Venezuela (1814); President of the Republic of Colombia, known as Gran Colombia (elected 1819; resignation accepted 1830); dictator of Peru (from 1824); named president of Bolivia (1825)
facts.known: leading the Spanish American wars of independence in northern South America; the crossing of the Andes and the Battle of Boyacá in 1819; founding the Republic of Colombia (Gran Colombia); the Jamaica Letter, Cartagena Manifesto and Angostura Address; the title El Libertador; Bolivia being named after him

t: Born into one of the wealthiest creole families of Caracas and orphaned as a child, Bolívar swore in Rome in 1805 to end Spanish rule in the Americas.

After two failed Venezuelan republics and exile in Jamaica and Haiti, he crossed the Andes in 1819 and, with his allies, defeated the Spanish in New Granada, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia by 1825.
He united Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador and Panama as the Republic of Colombia, but grew increasingly authoritarian and disillusioned, and died in 1830 as the union broke apart.
dyk: On 25 September 1828 Bolívar escaped assassins in Bogotá when Manuela Sáenz bought him time to flee the Palacio de San Carlos. He spent the night hiding under a bridge until loyal soldiers rescued him.
ev: On the Mons Sacer in Rome, Bolívar swears to end Spanish rule in the Americas
He launches the Admirable Campaign, issues the Decree of War to the Death, enters Caracas and is named "The Liberator"
He resigns his command in New Granada, sails into exile on Jamaica and writes the Jamaica Letter
He crosses the Andes, routs the Royalists at the Battle of Boyacá and is elected president of the new Republic of Colombia
With José Antonio Páez he decisively defeats the Royalists at the Battle of Carabobo and enters Caracas
Named dictator of Peru by its congress, he defeats José de Canterac at the Battle of Junín
He assumes supreme power as "president-liberator" of Colombia and survives an assassination attempt in Bogotá
His resignation is accepted in April; he dies of tuberculosis near Santa Marta in December

sections.early:
Simón Bolívar was born on 24 July 1783 in Caracas, capital of the Captaincy General of Venezuela, the fourth and youngest child of Juan Vicente Bolívar y Ponte and María de la Concepción Palacios y Blanco. The first of the family in the Americas, a notary from Spain's Basque Country also named Simón de Bolívar, had arrived in Venezuela in the 1580s, and by 1783 the Bolívars were among the wealthiest and most prestigious criollo (creole) families in the Spanish Americas. The British historian John Lynch described his childhood as "at once privileged and deprived". His father died of tuberculosis on 19 January 1786 and his mother on 6 July 1792. Following colonial custom the children were raised by African house slaves; Simón was raised by a slave named Hipólita.

Notoriously unruly as a child, he was taught by the educator Simón Rodríguez and the intellectual Andrés Bello, among others. In 1799 he was sent to Madrid, where he was educated in the Classics, literature and social studies. There he met María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaysa, daughter of another wealthy Caracas creole; they married on 26 May 1802 and sailed for Venezuela, where she died of yellow fever on 22 January 1803. Bolívar later said that he swore never to remarry.

He returned to Europe that year. He was in Paris when Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor of the French in 1804, and in April 1805 he set out with Rodríguez on a Grand Tour of Italy. On 18 August 1805, on the Mons Sacer in Rome, he swore to end Spanish rule in the Americas. He was back in Venezuela in June 1807.
sections.rise:
Napoleon's invasion of the Iberian peninsula in 1807–08 weakened Spanish authority. On 19 April 1810 the creoles of Caracas deposed the government of Vicente Emparán and created a Supreme Junta. Bolívar joined its diplomatic mission to Britain, which won no recognition, but he persuaded the revolutionary Francisco de Miranda to return. Congress declared Venezuela's independence on 5 July 1811. After an earthquake devastated the first republic on 26 March 1812, a Royalist army overran the west. Bolívar lost the fortress of Puerto Cabello, Miranda capitulated, and Bolívar left for Curaçao and then Cartagena.

In the service of the United Provinces of New Granada he issued the Cartagena Manifesto and secured the Magdalena River. On 14 May 1813 he launched the Admirable Campaign, entered Caracas on 6 August and was named "The Liberator". He became dictator of a Second Republic on 2 January 1814, but it was overwhelmed by slave revolts and the llanero army of José Tomás Boves, who occupied Caracas on 16 July. After further service in New Granada, Bolívar sailed for Jamaica in May 1815, where he wrote the Jamaica Letter.

In Haiti, President Alexandre Pétion gave him money and military supplies after Bolívar pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied. A first expedition in 1816 failed. Returning to Venezuela at the end of that year, he joined the Guayana campaign; Angostura fell on 17 July 1817 and became the provisional Republican capital, and on 30 January 1818 José Antonio Páez, who controlled most of the western Llanos, recognised him as supreme leader.
sections.deeds:
The congress that met at Angostura on 15 February 1819 heard Bolívar advocate a centralised government modelled on the British and elected him president the next day. On 27 May he marched toward the Andes. The army made a gruelling crossing of the Eastern Range, descended into New Granada on 6 July and routed the Royalists at the Battle of Boyacá on 7 August; Bolívar entered Bogotá three days later. On 17 December 1819 the congress decreed the Republic of Colombia, uniting Venezuela, New Granada and the still Spanish-held Quito, with Bolívar as president.

After a truce with the Spanish general Pablo Morillo in November 1820, fighting resumed, and on 24 June 1821 Bolívar and Páez decisively defeated the Royalists at the Battle of Carabobo. Panama declared independence that November and joined Colombia. Antonio José de Sucre won the Battle of Pichincha on 24 May 1822 and occupied Quito, and Bolívar secured Guayaquil for Colombia before meeting the Argentine general José de San Martín there in July; their conference produced no agreement.

Asked several times by the Peruvian congress to take command, Bolívar reached Lima on 1 September 1823 and was named dictator of Peru on 10 February 1824. He defeated José de Canterac at Junín on 6 August, and on 9 December Sucre defeated the viceroy's army at Ayacucho and accepted the surrender of all Royalist forces in Peru. On 6 August 1825 a congress in Chuquisaca declared Upper Peru the nation of Bolivia, named Bolívar its president and asked him to write a constitution, which was ratified with modification in July 1826.
sections.opponents:
Bolívar's methods and ambitions made enemies among Republicans as well as Royalists. In 1812 he was among the officers who arrested Miranda at La Guaira on charges of treason after Miranda's capitulation; Miranda passed into Spanish custody and died in a prison in Cádiz in 1816, and Bolívar received a passport for his role in the arrest. In the Admirable Campaign he issued the Decree of War to the Death, ordering the death of all Spaniards in South America not actively aiding his forces.

Rival commanders resisted him repeatedly. In 1814 Manuel Piar declared him a traitor and José Félix Ribas accused him of treachery and exiled him, and in 1816 Santiago Mariño and José Francisco Bermúdez deposed him. In 1817 Piar began fomenting rebellion, alleging that Bolívar had dismissed him because of his mulatto heritage; he was captured and executed by firing squad at Angostura on 16 October. In 1824 the Colombian congress stripped Bolívar of his authority for accepting the dictatorship of Peru. Peru's elites chafed at his rule and the presence of his soldiers, and in 1827 his opponents there deposed him and repealed his constitution.

His political ideas drew the same charge. He held that Spanish America needed a strong, centralised government, thought it necessary to rule as a dictator to avoid racial conflict and civil war, and intended to be president for life. The first historical evaluations of him were negative, criticising his conduct of the war, the execution of Piar, the betrayal of Miranda and his authoritarianism, and these criticisms endure in studies of him.
sections.last:
Bolívar left Peru in September 1826 in response to pleas for his return to Colombia, where Páez had revolted against Vice President Francisco de Paula Santander. He granted Páez an amnesty and confirmed his authority in Venezuela in January 1827; the amnesty, and clashes over Colombia's finances, turned his differences with Santander into open enmity. At the Convention of Ocaña in 1828, which seemed likely to adopt a federalist system, his allies walked out and left it without a quorum. On 27 August 1828 he assumed supreme power as "president-liberator" and abolished the vice presidency.

On 25 September 1828 a group of young liberals tried to assassinate him in Bogotá; Manuela Sáenz, bought time for his escape. Santander, whom Bolívar thought responsible, was pardoned but exiled, and Admiral José Prudencio Padilla, though uninvolved, was executed for an earlier rebellion. While Bolívar was away in 1829 his ministers planned for a Bourbon prince to succeed him as King of Colombia, a widely unpopular plan that he ordered stopped. Venezuelans voted to secede from Colombia.

He submitted his resignation to the congress that met in Bogotá on 20 January 1830; it was accepted on 27 April. He left Bogotá on 8 May, meaning to go into exile, and reached Cartagena in late June. With his health failing and no ship forthcoming, he was moved to the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino near Santa Marta, where he died of tuberculosis on 17 December 1830, aged 47. That year he declared to the Venezuelan general Juan José Flores, "all who have served the Revolution have plowed the sea."
sections.legacy:
Bolívar is regarded as a hero and a national and cultural icon throughout Latin America, and in the English-speaking world he is known as Latin America's George Washington. Bolivia and the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela bear his name, as do their currencies, the boliviano and the bolívar. His body was interred at Santa Marta in 1830; in 1842 Páez secured its return to Caracas, and in October 1876 it was moved to the National Pantheon of Venezuela.

From 1842 popular opinion of him in Venezuela became overwhelmingly positive and grew into what scholars have described as the "cult of Bolívar", led by successive heads of state. President Hugo Chávez made extensive use of his image and changed the country's official name to the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. Chávez also claimed that Bolívar had been poisoned; a commission exhumed the remains on 16 July 2010, and its results, made public in 2011, were inconclusive. In Colombia, allegiance or opposition to Bolívar formed the bedrock of the Conservative and Liberal parties respectively, and in 1974 the insurgent 19th of April Movement stole a sword said to be his from his Bogotá residence.

His writings remain central to his reputation: the Jamaica Letter has been called a "blueprint of Bolívar's political thought" and the Cartagena Manifesto "one of the great documents of Latin American history". He hoped for a federation of Latin American republics, and at Angostura argued for the abolition of slavery. In 1978 UNESCO created the International Simón Bolívar Prize.

summary: Simón Bolívar, a wealthy creole of Caracas, led the wars that freed Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain between 1810 and 1825 and joined several of them in the Republic of Colombia. His rule turned authoritarian, his union broke apart, and he died in 1830 on his way into exile.
